name: Frederik IX of Denmark
summary: Frederik IX accepted parliamentary constitutional monarchy and personally approved democratic reforms described by his biographers. His public addresses emphasized civic responsibility, international cooperation, peacekeeping and assistance to poorer countries, while offering little detailed economic or social policy.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The 1968 PDF explicitly calls for strengthening the UN and its peacekeeping capacity.

democracy-best.rationale: The 1968 PDF praises the liberties democracy provides and urges citizens, especially the young, to strengthen the democratic system.

direct-votes.rationale: His biography specifically reports approval of expanded referendums as protection for parliamentary minorities, rather than replacement of parliament.

duties-before-rights.rationale: He criticized a mentality concerned only with demanding rights and urged citizens to elevate duty, sacrifice and community.

national-self-determination.rationale: The attributed 1965 PDF explicitly endorses the freedom of nations and recognition of peoples’ right to self-determination.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The 1965 PDF explicitly welcomes Danish participation in NATO and international cooperation, rather than ending those commitments.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The 1968 PDF advocates further expanding assistance to developing countries and Denmark’s participation in that effort.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: He consistently accepted the monarch’s representative constitutional role and insisted that a government must have parliamentary backing.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: His addresses endorse working with allies and specifically welcome NATO membership alongside peacekeeping and détente.

dynastic-succession.rationale: He changed his earlier opposition to female succession and personally accepted his daughter becoming heir under the revised succession law.

second-chamber.rationale: His scholarly biography reports that he personally approved abolition of the upper chamber in the 1953 reforms.

notes: No inferred answers. Formal assent to the 1953 constitution and laws, NATO accession and developments occurring during his reign are not themselves treated as his positions. The biography explicitly distinguishes reforms he personally approved and records his insistence on parliamentary backing for government. Reviewed New Year addresses from 1955, 1965, 1968 and 1971 across all statement themes and checked the complete remaining null list. General compassion, peace wishes and praise for social security do not establish specific health, welfare, weapons or liberty policies. Danske Taler’s HTML versions of the 1965 and 1968 addresses omit passages present in their attributed PDF versions; relevant PDF evidence is identified by its exact URL, and confidence for positions depending on those omitted passages is limited to medium.
